column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The article contradicts itself on the temple: a Sun temple on the western bank (lead) and on the east side of the lake (Tomara section). Left the side out. The article also says the tank 'is also said' to have been built in 686 AD by Surajmal, son of Anang Pal I; this disagrees with the entry's 10th-century Surajpal, so it was left out. Visitor figures differ within the article (160,000 or 200,000 foreigners); used the dated 2015 figure.
Coronation date given as 16 March or 29 March 1368 in the article; written as March 1368. Chronicles disagree on the mother of Tarabya (Khame Mi or Shin Saw Gyi); left out.

The entry names the Narrensprung of Rottweil and the intangible heritage listing; neither is in the article, so not repeated or expanded. The article is loosely written and partly contradictory on when the distinct Swabian-Alemannic form developed (19th-century revival vs 'first quarter of the 20th century'); I kept to the dated founding of the VSAN.

The article says he is 'thought to have arrived' at Akkalkot in September or October 1856; the entry says 'about 1856', so no disagreement. Akkalkot royal family not in the article. The quotation 'Don't be afraid...' stands at the head of the article without a source line; it is attributed to him only implicitly. Kept as a saying of his followers' tradition.

SKIPPED: article too thin: a lead of about 120 words and a genealogy; nothing to add beyond the description The article says he was crowned at the age of 23 (born 1 December 1893, so 1916 or 1917); the entry says he reigned from 1915.

The article gives no year; the entry's 'around 517 BCE' is not contradicted. Heading 'Career' used for his rule, as he was a vassal tyrant rather than a monarch in the guide's sense; 'Reign' could also fit.

Left out the article's claim that the family descended from 'the Bulchan clan who were guardians of Atil in Khazaria': it is unsourced, implausible and probably vandalism. The heading 'Death and legacy' was not used: his death is told only in one sentence within Career.

The article dates the conflict 629–630; the entry gives 630, the year of the decisive defeat. The year of the opening offensive (13 December) is the 629 of the lead, written as such. The article contradicts itself on where the Turks were first resettled: 'the Ordos plateau and north of the Yellow River' in the lead, 'the Ordos plateau south of the Yellow River' in the aftermath; written without the river.

The entry says he ruled from Hierapolis-Castabala; the article says Pompey gave Castabala to Cappadocia and Anazarbus, the site of the mint, became the administrative centre, with Castabala perhaps returning only after c. 52 BC. Left the seat of rule out. The entry dates Pompey's recognition to 64 BCE; the article says 'in or after 66 BC' and the settlement of 66-63 BC, and that it may have been his father Strato who was confirmed. Written without a year.

The article is on the Luwian Tarḫunz and treats the Hittite Tarḫunna as a closely associated god; the entry treats Tarhunt as the storm god of the Hittites and other Anatolian peoples. Written so that the Luwian details are marked as Luwian; the entry's claims on Hittite kingship are not in the article and were not touched.

The entry states that Shō Hashi conquered Sannan and defeated Taromai in 1429. The article treats 1429 as Sai On's (1725) inference ('naïvely inferred'), says the Chinese did not know when or how the king disappeared, notes the Chūzan Seikan places the overthrow of Sannan before 1421, and reports Wada Hisanori's hypothesis that Taromai was Shō Hashi's eldest son and Ōōso a pseudonym or puppet of Shō Hashi. These points contradict the entry and were left out; the entry may need revising. The entry calls the kingdom Nanzan; the article uses the reading Sannan, used here.

Death and legacy is used although the killing itself is told in Reign; the description already gives the murder in 54 BCE. Left out the long digression on badger lore and Welsh games, which concerns the name only.
The entry says he founded Tanjung Puteri, later Johor Bahru; the article says he renamed the territory Iskandar Puteri and administered it from Teluk Belanga. Left the naming out.

The article names Thado Minbya's chief consort as 'Saw Omma of Pinya, the chief queen of the last three Pinya kings', while the Swa Saw Ke article makes his queen Saw Omma the sister of Swa Saw Ke; I have named only 'his queen Saw Omma' without her origin. British colonial-era claims that his father was Shan are disputed in the article; left out.

SKIPPED: article thin (about 300 words) and self-contradictory on the key dates; too little that can be told without disagreeing with the entry Death: the lead gives 27 August 1648, the body says he died on 19 October 1648 after his brother Minye Kyawswa died on 28 August 1648. Capital: the article says he moved it to Ava in 1634; the entry says 1635. Accession: the entry dates his reign from 1629; the article says he and Minye Kyawswa took Pegu and executed Minyedeippa in 1630. The article does not mention the revenue inquest, the service groups or the Kaunghmudaw pagoda.
The article gives the Gaelic title as 'Cuckoo of the Tree' in the lead and 'The Cuckoo in the Grove' later; not translated here.
SKIPPED: article of about 330 words, nearly all of it already in the description; nothing substantial to add

The article says that at the temple of the Dioscuri at Phoebeon 'epheboi were sacrificed'; this probably means the young men sacrificed there (Pausanias), so it was left out as unclear. The article is short (about 280 words); the text stays close to it.
The entry's figure of some 500 followers is not in the article; not repeated.
Left out the article's rankings (film lists, Southern Weekly's top ten songs) and its description of Taiwan's government at the time, under the guide's rule on rankings and verdicts.

SKIPPED: the article contradicts the entry on the central facts of his death: it dates it to 203 BCE and has him killed fighting the Han general Han Xin at Lixia after a guerrilla war, where the entry has him killed in 205 BCE fleeing Xiang Yu's invasion; with the death left out, too little remains beyond the description Article: died 203 BC, killed in the rout at Lixia by Han scouts or defectors after Han Xin's invasion of winter 204 BC. Entry: d. 205 BCE, killed as he fled Xiang Yu's invasion. The article also dates his revolt against Xiang Yu's kings to 205 BC (when Liu Bang's coalition rose) and has Tian Jia, not Tian Heng's line, holding Jimo in 202 BC; its account looks confused and needs a second source.

The article contradicts itself and the entry on dates: it says the area was populated in 25 AD and abandoned by the Igneri in 600, then reoccupied by Taínos in 1000, and elsewhere gives continuous occupation from 400 to 1000; the entry says the courts were built from around 600 by pre-Taíno and early Taíno peoples. All occupation dates left out. It also gives seven ball courts in one place and nine ball fields in another; no count given. The article says the cemetery's skeletons are 'most from the Igneri and the rest from the pre-Taíno cultures', which is muddled; only the Igneri majority kept.

The article gives his birth as 1402 (Chiang Mai Chronicle); the entry has 1409. Left out. The article has his coronation on 24 March 1443; the entry has his reign from 1441. Left out, as is the article's 'when he was 32 years old', which depends on the birth year. The 1477 council at Wat Chet Yot is not in the article.

The article uses both Muyquytá and Bacatá for his capital; I used the name only where the article ties it to the event. The prophecy of Popón is told without a source in the article; I framed it as the chronicles' account.

The article spells the second office tlacateccatl; the entry has tlacatecatl. I followed the article's spelling. The article treats Moctezuma Ilhuicamina and Moctezuma I as one person; kept as it says.
The article gives his death as 21 August 1937, in line with the entry's year.
The article says Huayna Capac was probably born in Tumebamba; the entry says 'said to have been born there'. Not repeated. The founding of Cuenca in 1557 is not in the article.

The article dates a set of Travancore peace terms to 17 February 1742, apparently out of sequence with the talks of 1742-1743; left out. The Mukkuvar fishermen's folk tales of the battle were left out for length.

The article contradicts itself on the day of signing: its lead says 25 April 1809, the treaty text quoted in it says 26 April. Written as April 1809. The lead also mentions a proclamation finalising the transaction on 3 May 1809; left out as its relation to the treaty text is unclear.
The article mentions a present-day movement for unification that would invalidate the treaty; left out as it is written as still going on.
The article's conversion of the compensation into 2025 dollars was left out.

The article says Britain 'guaranteed Bhutan's independence' and calls Bhutan one of the few Asian kingdoms never conquered; left out as a characterisation rather than a term of the text, which it prints in full.

The article says Tipu was 'unable to pay an indemnity of 330 lakhs' and therefore had to surrender two sons; the entry says he paid a heavy indemnity and handed over two sons. I wrote only that the treaty set the indemnity and required the hostages, without saying whether it was paid.
The article calls the Order's party the Teutonic Order; the entry says the Livonian Order, its branch. Not a contradiction; kept both as the article explains them.
The article lists the provinces of Oran, Koléa, Médéa, Tlemcen and Algiers as ruled by Abdelkader, while the entry says France kept Oran, Algiers and their hinterlands; the provinces were left out.
The article gives no dates for his journey, return or the founding of Buseoksa; the entry's 661, c. 670 and 676 stand unchallenged.
The entry says Riel's Métis seized the fort in November 1869; the article says late 1869. Written as late 1869, which agrees.

The article's 1799 Battle of Aluqair passage is muddled (it names Ibrahim Pasha as commander against the First Saudi State in 1799): left out. The article dates the Uqair mosque to the 16th century 'by archaeological surveys' and calls the Abu Zahmul tower possibly Ottoman: left out.

The article gives a reign of approximately 485 to 523; the end date is Hakobyan's estimate, so I attributed it. The Council of Aghuen (c. 488) in the entry is not in the article, so it is not repeated or contradicted.

The article has only one sentence of history (cantref, marcher lordship from 1282), so the text is weighted to geography. The entry says the vale runs from hills south of Ruthin to the sea at Rhyl; the article gives its length as some 20 miles from the coast, consistent.

The article names Arnefrit’s father as the Friulian Duke Lupa; kept in that form. The article's sentence identifying Alcioka with a figure who went to Friuli 'with her escort in 662' is garbled and was left out. The article says Slavs of the Eastern Alps joined Samo 'at the latest after the weakening of Pannonian Avars in 626 (if not already in 623)'.

The article dates his coronation to 628 and says he reigned 'from 628 until at least 654'; the entry says 'around 630' and calls him a Sasanian vassal, while the article says he gained the trust of Heraclius when crowned. I gave no year for the coronation and did not call him either vassal or Byzantine client. The article's lead sentence 'The last holder of the title was Vachagan III' is garbled (Vachagan III was the last Arsacid king, before the Mihranids); left out. Its family list mixes children and grandchildren; I named only the first five issues.
SKIPPED: article has under 200 words of substance (boundaries, two citations and a list of modern institutions named after the region) and adds little to the entry

SKIPPED: article too thin: about 250 words of substance beyond a literature list, much of it already in the entry; a text drafted from it came to about 220 words. Note for the editor: the article says part of Kirchwerder remained an exclave of the Prussian District of Harburg until the Greater Hamburg Act of 1938, while the entry says the district passed wholly to Hamburg in 1868.

The article spells the play both Harakeli and Harikeli Nataka; the entry uses Harakeli, and the text does not name it again. The article's figures for his army (1 million men etc.) come from his court poet's play and were left out as boastful.

The article says the Company's ship Restoration was among the Maratha ships at anchor and caught fire; the passage is muddled, so the text says only that the Angre fleet burned. Unconfirmed claims of an undersea tunnel and wall, and the local story of Lockyer and helium, were left out.

Reign dates c. 250-275 are the article's; the entry says 3rd century, consistent. The entry says the Puranas name him a Brahmin chief; the article says the Ajanta inscription calls him a dvija. Not contradicted.

The article gives his reign as 1234-1263; the entry says 1235-1263, so no starting year is given. The article names his killer Sadayavarman Sundara Pandyan I; the entry has Jatavarman Sundara Pandya I (the same king, two transliterations). I wrote only 'Sundara Pandyan I'.

The article says Venice's licence to print was granted in January 1611 under the original title; not needed. The entry calls Tuscan the model and mentions French and Spanish academies following it; the article does not discuss those, so nothing contradicts.
The article dates the war 1915-1917 and says small pockets of resistance continued until 1917; the entry dates it 1915-1916. The 1917 end and the pockets of resistance were left out.
Most of the article is already in the entry; the text adds the magistrate's working, the council's business and the drawing of lots.

The article gives c. 1615 - c. 1672; the entry gives fl. 1652, not contradicted. The article says he is 'credited with using the liberum veto for the first time'; the entry says the first successful exercise. Not repeated.

Left out the current membership list ('As of May 2025') and the 2024 appointments dispute; the 2023 claims against the Sixth National Government are only begun in the excerpt. The entry gives 1985 as the start of claims reaching back to 1840; the article agrees.

SKIPPED: article too thin (about 250 words) and partly self-contradictory: a text from it came to under 200 words. For the editor: the article gives birth c. 1210 and death aged about 60 (entry: c. 1230); says he succeeded his father in 1243 yet that his older brother Richard's lands were seized after Richard's death in 1247; and has him created earl in 1263 'by King Edward I' (entry: by Lord Edward in 1263 or 1264). It adds his death at Galway on 28 July 1271, his defeat with Walter de Ufford by Aedh mac Felim Ua Conchobair at Ath an Chip in 1270, and his marriage about 1257 to Avelina, daughter of Sir John Fitzgeoffrey.
The article's birth year c. 1634 is not in the entry; not contradicted. The article does not date Massasoit's death; the entry's 'around 1661' is not repeated.

The entry's Battle of Scheut is not in the article. The article's lead says Brabant had a tradition of male primogeniture while its background section says female succession under the ius Brabantinum had been applied several times; I gave only the background's account.
Article says the revolt 'began in 1462 and ended a decade later without definitive result', then was resolved in 1486; consistent with the entry's 1462-1486.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance: a list of kings and a note that their relationship is unknown, nothing the description lacks

The article names the founder of the present compound (1044) as King Athitayarat, the entry's Adityaraja; the name is left out of the text to avoid two spellings on one page. The article's lead says the temple's origins date from the 11th century; the 897 stupa is given as tradition ('is said to have built').

Birth year: the article gives 1144/1153, the entry c. 1144; no birth year is given in the text. The entry says John granted Gower in 1203; the article names the grant without a year, so the text does not mention Gower's date.

The article gives his birth as 22 February 1730 but says older works give 1731 (entry: c. 1730); no birth date in the text. The article contradicts itself on his death: 13 November 1813 in the lead, 17 November 1813 in the body; no day is given in the text.

Dates of office: the article's lead gives North Carolina 1764-1771 and New York 1771-1777 (the entry: 1765-1771 and 1771-1780). The body says he was acting lieutenant governor from 1764 and governor from 1765, and left for London in September 1780 while keeping the nominal title. The text gives 1765 for North Carolina and no end year for New York.

The article's lead says he was bishop of Passau from 1191 (as the entry), but its body says he was elected on 11 March 1190 and consecrated on 9 June; the text gives no year for his election or consecration.
Death: the article gives c. September 202 BC, the entry 201 BCE; the text gives no year for his death.
SKIPPED: thin article: length, a list of towns, two river restorations and a list of birds; no history of the valley or its towns to add
The entry gives 937 for Xu Zhigao's taking the throne; the excerpt gives no year, so the text does not date it.

The entry places Qin's victory over Tang at Qianshuiyuan; the article gives no place for Xue Ju's victory over Li Shimin and names Qianshuiyuan only for Li Shimin's later defeat of Zong Luohou. The text names no place for the first battle.
Left out the present-day statement attributed to Héctor Llaitul (a living person's current political claim).
The 1953 excavations are in the entry; added the second campaign and the critique. Left out the novels and the musical works.

The article spells the family names Yŏn Kaesomun, Yŏn Namgŏn, Yŏn Namsan (McCune-Reischauer); the entry uses Yeon Gaesomun. The text uses the article's spellings for the brothers and names the father only as Yŏn Kaesomun. The entry says he fled to the fortress of Gungnae; the article says only that he fled to the Tang. The entry dates his father's death 665 or 666; the article gives 665. Neither point is repeated in the text.

Death date: the article's lead says 19 January 1127, its body December 1126; the entry has 1126. The text says only that he died in exile at Yeonggwang. The article romanizes his name Yi Cha-gyŏm / Yi Chagyŏm (McCune-Reischauer); the entry's name is Yi Ja-gyeom. The text calls him Yi throughout and uses the article's spellings for other names.
The article says nothing about the book's contents (the countries described), so there is no Contents section.

The Arras culture and Deira, named in the entry, do not appear in the article. Left out the climate figures, sports clubs and the 2024 consultation on an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty (not concluded in the article).

The article's lead says Zabdas was executed at Emesa after the trial; its Death section says only that most officials were executed, which might have included Zabdas, since he is not mentioned afterwards. The text gives the trial and the executions of most officials without saying whether Zabdas was one of them.

Birth: the article's lead gives 1835, its body around 1835 or 1840; the entry has c. 1840. No birth year in the text. The article's account of Al Zorah dates Sharjah's appeal to 1890 within events of 1895-1897, an internal inconsistency; the episode is left out.
The article says the horde migrated from Kazakhstan; left out as unclear. The entry's 'Heavenly King of Wei in 388' agrees with the article.
Short article; the text adds the 387 and 390 campaigns, the Yecheng attack and the details of the 392 crossing.

The article says the song was first published in The Nation on 13 July 1844 (as the entry's dates), but also that its first publication was in the collection The Spirit of the Nation; the text avoids saying which was first.

The article dates the end of the Sarbuland campaign to VS 1787 and gives it as 1731 CE; the year was left out. Much of the article is bardic and heroic narrative (Kesari Singh, Jagram Singh), left out. The entry's Idar line of 1728 is not in the article. The article's figure of 100,000 at Gangwana is a bardic-sounding number; given only as 'a much larger force'.

The entry calls him the second caliph; the article calls him the third sultan and numbers his sons as the fifth and eleventh sultans. The ordinals were left out. The article names his sons Ahmadu Atiku and Abd ar-Rahman; the entry names Umaru Nagwamatse and Abubakar II Atiku na Raba. Whether Ahmadu Atiku and 'Abubakar II Atiku na Raba' are one person was not checked.

Dating: the entry says the British Museum scroll is probably a copy of the fifth or sixth century; the article gives modern scholarship's range as the 5th to 8th century. The date was left out of the text. The article puts the acquisition in 1899 'during the aftermath of the Boxer Rebellion', which was in 1900; the year was left out.

The article's claim that Aflah converted the whole Maghreb to his doctrine and traded as far as Mali and Chad was left out as overstated. The article's sentence on al-Abbasiyya is garbled ('ordered the burning and razed an entire city named Al 'Abbasiyya by the Aghlabids'); read as a town founded by the Aghlabids.
Short article; the text adds the sources, the verses' story and the later uses.

The article gives his death as 1510; the entry's 'c. 1510' agrees closely. The article attributes the title's maternal inheritance to 'Kalinago culture', which looks like a slip for Taíno; the culture was not named.
The entry dates his death to 1510; the article says he died in 1508 or 1509. The year was left out of the text.

The entry says he took Ahlat in 1207. The article says his 1207 campaign failed to take Akhlat and that he took it after a second attempt in 1208, yet also that the Ayyubid rulers of Khilat styled themselves Shah-Armen 'from 1207 onwards'. The year was left out of the text.

The article's lead says he was governor from 10 July 1901, but its body says he became deputy governor that day and was appointed governor on 20 November 1902, as the entry's 1902-1914 has it; the body was followed. The article says he founded Rabaul in 1903 and the government moved there by 1910; the entry's 1910 move agrees.
The entry's dates c. 1750-1793 agree with the article's 15 December 1750 - 17 February 1793.

The entry dates the refounding to around 1484; the article puts his arrival at Tetouan in 1491 and after the fall of Granada, and has him holding Piñar until 1485. These years were left out of the text. The entry calls Sayyida al-Hurra his daughter-in-law; the article calls Sidi al-Mandri II his grandson or nephew. The relationship was left unstated. The entry's Wattasid permission is not in the article.

The article's lead says he was not caught until 1707; its body says he surrendered at Surabaya in 1708, as the entry has it. The body was followed. The article says he died 26 years after his exile, or some three decades after his fall, in 1734 (the entry's date).
The article says Cakraningrat IV became Amangkurat IV's son-in-law.

The article's lead dates al-Mansur's rule from 976, its list of hajibs from 981; the entry says 'from the 970s'. The start year was left out. Short article made mostly of ruler lists; written as prose from them.

The article says Pedro IV was crowned in São Salvador on 2 August 1696 but that the restoration took place only in 1709; the coronation date was not repeated. The article's pronouns in the plot of 1696 are confused ('in order to oust him', 'two of his captains'); read as referring to the queen.
Entry says datu from 1935; the article gives no year for his accession, so none is given here. Award name spelled as the source gives it (Satyalacana Karya; usually Satyalancana).

Entry calls him mormaer; the article calls him king of Moray. Kept 'king of Moray' as the article's title for the line, without contradicting the entry's description. Article is short (about 300 words); text kept near the lower limit.
Article gives the periodical's name both as Journal Economique and Journal Oeconomique; used the latter from the Writings section.

Entry says he fought at Ochakiv and Izmail; the article names only Berezan, so only Berezan is mentioned. Article gives birth 'between 1732 and 1744' but also 'aged 24, 1756'; birth year left out. Article dates the coronation delegation to 1764 (Catherine II was crowned in 1762); year left out.

Article calls Mitsunao and Mitsusada his sons in one sentence and his brothers in the next; their relation is left out. Article dates the Mutsu/Dewa grant to 1392 from Yoshimochi; the Ujimitsu article dates it 1391 from Yoshimitsu. Year and grantor left out. Date Masamune here is a 14th-century namesake, not the famous Sengoku lord; named without further description.

Article says he died at the age of 41, which does not fit the entry's 1359–1398 (or the article's own dates); age at death left out. Article dates the Yamana campaign alliance to 1391; the Mitsukane article dates the grant to 1392. Year left out.

Article says the assembly suspended the Oriental deputies on 5 March 1813 but that they were elected on 21 April 1813; the order is impossible, so both dates are left out. Article gives the end of the sessions both as 24 January 1815 (lead) and 26 January 1815 (final session); used the final-session date, which matches the fifth period.

Article gives 950–1020; entry says 10th–11th century. Her death year is not given here; birth year not stated either. Spellings follow the source: Samayparikshe, Vajjivamsa (also Vajiivamsa there), Dandnayaka, Paduvala Tailap.
Entry gives the Etruscan name as Avle Vipinas; the article gives Avile Vipina. Neither repeated in the text. Article says the bucchero is coeval with the reign of Servius Tullius.
Article spells the tribe both Abrincatui (lead) and Abrincuti (history); used Abrincatui.

Article says the British restored him to the throne the year after 1762, but also that he returned to Sulu only after Azim ud-Din II's death; the British restoration is left out. Article gives his abdication as 1774 (lead) and November 1773 (body); year left out.

SKIPPED: article too thin: about 250 words, much of it already in the description (accession, trade, Siamese tribute) Article says he overthrew his cousin 'Sultan Muhammad II of Kelantan' in 1839, apparently a slip for Terengganu. Article: born 1806; joint sultan with Mansur Shah II in 1831; banished to Daik in 1833; Istana Hijau built 1870.
Entry says he created a bishopric for the Curonians in 1234; the article does not mention it, so nothing is said either way.

Article dates Giberto's death to 1585 but later says she was widowed in 1596; no date given for her widowhood. Article oddly calls Ottavio Farnese 'Duke of Colorno' as the one who invested Girolamo; investor left out.
Article gives his rule as 665–680 CE; entry has 7th century, consistent.
The article is short (about 300 words); this text uses nearly all of it. The article gives the founding as 1872, consistent with the entry's early 1870s.
The article also gives Tesseneiei among the towns abandoned; left out for length. The comparison with El Alamein is left out.
The article's lead says 16 tribal leaders were imprisoned; its body says between 13 and 16. The text gives the range.

The article also says Legazpi gave Manila the title of city on 19 May 1571 (certified 19 June 1572); the entry says he formally founded it as a Spanish city later in June. The May date is left out; only the municipal government of 24 June is given. The two quoted Spanish accounts give 70 and 80 Spaniards for the expedition; left out.
The article's lead dates the second battle 15-16 April, while its account of the battle says it began on 13 April. The text says mid-April.

The article dates the battle 1-2 April 1885; the entry says it was fought on 2 April. The 1 April artillery bombardment is described as coming the day before the main assault, without calling it a day of the battle.

DATE: the article gives 9 January 1887 (and calls it Ethiopian Christmas); the entry gives 6 January 1887. No day is printed; the text says only that the emir attacked on the Ethiopian Christmas. The article contradicts itself on the hour of the attack (early morning, a night attack, fire opened at 11:00 am); times left out.
The article gives the distance to the Cape as six hundred kilometres in one place and King's ride as 960 kilometres in another; no distance is printed.

LOCATION: the article places the battle on the upper Terelj river, 60 km east of Ulaanbaatar; the entry places it near the Tuul River south-east of Ulaanbaatar. No river or direction is printed. The article's lead says Qing armies were personally led by the emperor, but its account has Fiyanggu's army fighting after the emperor turned back; the text follows the account, as the entry does.
The article says Waali ordered seven gunpowder stores fired and six went up; the entry speaks of the city's gunpowder store in the singular. No number of stores is printed.
NUMBERING: the article calls Boabdil Muhammad XI of Granada and names his rival Muhammad XII; the entry calls Boabdil Muhammad XII. The text calls him Boabdil only and does not name the rival.

The article is not consistent about the garrison's end: its lead and later passages say Balbhadra led about 70 survivors out fighting, while one passage says 50 or 60 men remained and dragged their officers away. The text follows the 70 version given in the lead.

The date of the decisive fighting is given differently: Gupta treats it as 14 March 1823, while another account says the battle lasted two days and one night. The text gives no day for the main battle.
The article mentions no mural; nothing about it is added.

The article is thin on the battle itself; it says Rajmahal had been under siege for about four months by Husain Quli Beg, which reads oddly beside the Mughals proceeding towards it, so that point is left out.
The article calls the Eastern Wei army more than twenty times larger and the victory miraculous; this is left out, and the reported strengths are given with the article's own hedge.

The article calls it one of the bloodiest battles on Lower Saxon territory; the entry says of sixteenth-century Germany. Neither phrase is repeated. Maurice's death by friendly fire is given only as an allegation, as the article has it.

The article places the battle off Qingdao and gives no month; the entry's 'late 1161' and 'later that month' are not repeated. The article gives the Song navy's growth without precise dates ('in one century').

The article says proposals for the date range from the end of the seventh century BC to after 510 BC; the entry dates the battle to the 6th century BCE and says Croton recovered to destroy Sybaris in 510 BCE, so the range's ends are left out. Strabo's view that the battle's losses caused Croton's decline is left out, as it sits uneasily with the entry's statement that Croton recovered.

The entry says al-Musta'in was defeated by the forces of Alfonso I; the article doubts that Alfonso was present in person. The text keeps to the forces (knights of Aragon and Pamplona) and reports the dispute over Alfonso's own presence, which does not contradict the entry. The article gives 1 Rajab 503 AH as the Islamic date.

The article's dates conflict among themselves: medical study at Edinburgh 'from 1892' but a Bachelor of Medicine dated 1889 in the honours list; FRSE in 1900 in the text but 1909 in the honours list; a 'formal accession in 1888' and a 50th anniversary of accession in 1934 against succession in 1869.
